#8993. Single Women Deserve Honeymoons Too—Here’s How to Plan One

I’m on a speedboat whizzing towards my latest vacation destination. As we bounce along, I attempt to take a selfie. The shot I want is the waves, the boats, the islands, but I can’t seem to get the kissing couples out the background. No matter which way I turn, there are honeymooners in my viewfinder. The boat operators and I are the only single people on this vessel. Technically I, too, am a part of a couple—actually, a throuple of single girlfriends heading for an Anguilla getaway. The trip is what I like to call a we-moon.

So often we have our dream destinations on reserve for the day we can go with the person we’ve agreed to spend our life with. There’s the honeymoon and the babymoon, but when do single women get to celebrate life milestones and fulfill the desire for companionship and adventure? That’s the we-moon.

For my most recent we-moon, I was invited to the Four Seasons Resort and Residences Anguilla and joined by two girlfriends. Now, you are probably wondering: What is the difference between this and your average girls trip? Well, similar to a honeymoon or babymoon, a we-moon is taken to celebrate a big life milestone. For me, it was my first book. Single women are so often traveling to celebrate others for their bachelorette or wedding or baby shower. Rarely do we get friends to travel and celebrate something that doesn’t fit into the typical timeline.

That is the purpose of a we-moon. It’s making the phone call to ask your friends to travel and celebrate an achievement with you, just like you do for others. It could be a promotion, a new job, a masters degree, or a book deal.

When crafting the perfect we-moon, there are things to keep in mind to make sure that the trip goes smoothly. I spoke to Joy Harden Bradford, PhD, author of Sisterhood Heals about the best way to pull off a destination celebration with no drama.

“I think having a place where everybody can retreat and have alone time is really good if that is something that the group can do. So private sleeping quarters are important,” she says. “Also having conversations about budget ahead of time. Because some people [might say], ‘Oh, we don't need a five-star hotel. We’re just going to be there to sleep. We’re going to be out.’ And other people are like, ‘No, I like luxury.’ So you don’t want to wait until you get there to find out that there’s a difference in the group about that.”

Another thing you should talk about ahead of time is how many group excursions everyone is down to do. “Because I think for a lot of us, there’s so much going on in our regular life that there’s a lot of expectations for what a vacation should be,” says Dr. Bradford. “‘It’s the one time I get to get away,’ and so people really put a lot on it.”

There are many different vacation styles. We’ve all been on a trip that is overplanned and leaves you more exhausted than when you left. Everyone should discuss what activities they want to do, and a good portion should be optional. For example, we worked on an itinerary with our villa concierge. When it came time to do the private yoga session poolside, some people wanted to rest. So I locked in for a one-on-one session, in which I was able to pay extra attention to modifications and my personal pain points. There were plenty of things that we did together, like an afternoon at the spa, where we all got Anguilla-themed massages, and an excursion across the island in a Jeep to see a different beach. Sometimes you just want to take a nap on vacation, and that is okay.

Me doing yoga with my instructor by the villa pool.

One of the things we did as a group was a margarita-making class. The three of us lined up at the bar of the villa and learned how to properly shake and measure lime juice, orange liqueur, and tequila. Research says that picking up a new skill is good for your brain health. (Although I’m not sure they meant consuming three margaritas in an hour….) The new experience for you can be learning a new sport like pickleball, going to a cooking class, or even playing board games by the beach. This is even better when it becomes a social experiment because even if you fail, you can laugh it off with friends.

What is a girls trip without girl talk? You have to set the mood for conversations. It’s not always a good time to dive deep into your last breakup as you are sitting at a noisy restaurant or relaxing at a spa appointment. But when you are away from your regular routine, there is a great opportunity to open up. “If these are people that you’re actually hoping to grow closer to, then it is important to continue to go deeper with those relationships. And that really requires a lot of vulnerability, which is really hard for people,” says Bradford. “Girls trips really provide a great opportunity and a great backdrop because you are away from your regular routine to maybe get into some of those things that you don’t have time to talk about later.” You have to set the mood for your friends to unravel. For me, I planned a night in the villa's private jacuzzi tub, watching the sunset, and drinking wine. That’s where we shared our work woes and dating troubles as a night cap.

My friends and I having girl talk by the fire.

Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from New York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA

Here's the critical nuance that trips up new users: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

Avios are one of the most accessible award currencies in the ecosystem. You can transfer from four major transferable points programs at a 1:1 ratio:

Marriott Bonvoy also transfers to Avios at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Avios), and Marriott throws in a 5,000 Avios bonus for every 60,000 Marriott points transferred. That's a less efficient path for this redemption, but worth knowing.

The 355-day booking window means you can transfer and book nearly a full year in advance — critical for holiday travel or high-demand routes.

British Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. That means you could theoretically fly into one city and out of a nearby city without paying for two separate awards — useful if you're exploring a region and want flexibility. For short domestic hops, this opens up creative itinerary options that pure point-to-point programs don't allow.

Before you touch your Avios balance, go to aa.com and run a standard flight search for your route. When the results load, look specifically for flights labeled 'Web Special' or filter by lowest MileSAAver awards. You're searching for American's own award inventory — the same inventory British Airways can see and book. If AA shows saver-level availability (the lowest award tier), British Airways will almost certainly be able to book it too.

This step saves you frustration. Don't transfer points until you've confirmed the flight you want is bookable at the saver level.

Double-check that your route qualifies for the 7,500 Avios tier by confirming it's under 650 miles. NYC to Boston is about 187 miles. LAX to SFO is about 337 miles. Both qualify easily. A quick Google search — '[City A] to [City B] flight distance miles' — gives you the straight-line distance. When in doubt, routes you'd describe as 'short regional hops' within the same metro corridor will almost always qualify.

Go to britishairways.com, log into (or create) your Executive Club account, and run an Avios award search for the same route and dates. You should see the American Airlines flight(s) appear at 7,500 Avios + a small tax amount — typically $5–$15. If the flight shows up here, you're ready to book.

Once you've confirmed availability, it's time to transfer. Here's what to do based on your points currency:

Important: Only transfer what you need. Points transferred to British Airways cannot be moved back.

Return to BA's award search (refresh if needed), select your American Airlines flight, and complete the booking. You'll pay the Avios from your balance plus the small tax amount with a credit card. You'll receive an American Airlines confirmation number, which you can use at aa.com to manage your reservation, select seats, and add TSA PreCheck or Known Traveler Numbers.

Let's make this concrete. It's mid-October and you want to visit a college friend in Boston for the weekend — flying out of New York's JFK on a Friday evening, returning Sunday afternoon.

You pull up Google Flights. Friday evening nonstops from JFK to BOS? The cheapest is $189. The convenient 6:30 PM departure on American Airlines is $229. Sunday afternoon return is another $199. Round-trip cash cost: $428.

You check aa.com and confirm both flights show saver-level award availability. You open British Airways' site and find:

You transfer 15,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to British Airways — it arrives instantly. You book both flights through BA, receive your AA confirmation numbers, and log into aa.com to select your seats.

If those flights had crept up to $300 each (not unusual around Columbus Day weekend), you'd be looking at 4 cents per point — outstanding for a domestic economy booking.

You're on a standard American Airlines narrow-body — likely a Boeing 737 or Airbus A319. It's economy, which for a 45-minute flight is entirely appropriate. You'll get a beverage service, overhead bin space, and you land at the same gate, use the same terminal, and have the same on-time performance as any other passenger on that plane. The difference is that they paid $229 and you paid $5.60 plus some points that cost you roughly $150 to earn through everyday spending.

That's the FI mindset applied to travel: same experience, radically different cost.

Do This: Book Up to 355 Days Out for Holiday Travel BA's booking window opens 355 days in advance, and American releases its best saver space early. If you're targeting Thanksgiving weekend, Christmas, or a peak summer Friday, set a calendar reminder to search at the 355-day mark. Award seats on popular routes at peak times go fast.

Do This: Use the Open-Jaw Rule Creatively BA allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. If you're flying into NYC but want to return from a different airport — say JFK inbound and EWR outbound — you may be able to structure this as a single open-jaw award rather than two separate bookings. Worth exploring for multi-city weekend trips.

Avoid This: Booking BA-Operated Flights with This Strategy This cannot be overstated — BA's own flights carry $300–800+ in carrier-imposed surcharges. If you accidentally book a British Airways codeshare or BA-metal flight instead of an American Airlines-operated flight, you'll owe hundreds in fees. Always verify the operating carrier before confirming. Look for 'Operated by American Airlines' in the booking details.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability Points transferred to British Airways are one-way and permanent. Never transfer until you have eyes on the specific flight, date, and saver availability you want. The 30-second search on BA's site before transferring is non-negotiable.

Do This: Keep Your Account Active Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you accumulate Avios for a future trip, make sure to earn or redeem at least a small amount every three years. Even a small shopping portal purchase through the BA Executive Club keeps your balance alive.

Do This: Stack with Other Short Hops Think about recurring trips in your life — quarterly visits to family, annual conferences, weekend trips to a nearby city. This sweet spot isn't just for one redemption; it's a repeatable system. A modest Avios balance of 30,000–45,000 points could cover three to six regional roundtrips per year.

Book the flight and add your AAdvantage number to the reservation so you receive any applicable elite benefits. You will receive a confirmation from British Airways, and the ticket will also appear in your AA account.

Yes. British Airways and American Airlines are both Oneworld alliance members, so you can use BA Avios to book award seats on AA-operated flights. You book directly through the British Airways website (ba.com) and search for AA flight numbers.

Not on domestic American Airlines flights. The typical fee is just $5.60 each way. High fuel surcharges only apply when booking British Airways-operated long-haul flights, not when using Avios on partner airlines like AA domestically.

This sweet spot was practically designed for the ChooseFI beginner — someone who has their first transferable points card (a Chase Sapphire Preferred, an Amex Gold, or a Bilt card) and wants to make a real, tangible redemption without navigating complex routing rules or praying for elusive premium cabin availability.

Minimum to get started: You need at least 7,500 Avios (or transferable points to convert) for a one-way. For a round-trip, 15,000. Most sign-up bonuses — even modest ones — cover multiple round-trips with this sweet spot.

Who this is NOT for: If you're flying coast-to-coast (NYC to LAX is over 2,400 miles — a different, higher Avios tier), this specific pricing won't apply. This sweet spot is purpose-built for short hops under 650 miles. It's also not the move if you already have AA elite status and can snag cheap upgrades — but for the rest of us, it's perfect.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness** — and that rating is fully deserved. Let's be specific about why. That's genuinely the whole checklist. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is the redemption to start with. You'll build the muscle memory — search, confirm, transfer, book — in about 20 minutes, and you'll have a nearly free flight to show for it. Welcome to travel rewards.

Though GLP-1 agonists can be beneficial for weight loss, it’s important to keep in mind that there is limited research on the long-term effects of these medications.

Additionally, research from 2022 suggests that weight regain is likely once you stop taking GLP-1 agonists.

Therefore, it’s best to pair GLP-1 agonists with modifications to your diet and lifestyle. A healthcare professional, such as a doctor or registered dietitian, can also provide ongoing guidance and support to promote long-term weight loss.

GLP-1 agonists are currently approved for three conditions: type 2 diabetes, obesity, and heart disease.

Keep in mind that these medications should be used alongside other lifestyle modifications, including changes to your diet and regular physical activity.

A doctor or other trusted healthcare professional can help determine whether a GLP-1 agonist may be beneficial for you, depending on your health concerns and goals.

Though GLP-1 agonists may support weight loss and help manage blood sugar levels, it’s important to be aware of the possible side effects, such as vomiting, stomach pain, fatigue, constipation or diarrhea, mood changes, and more.

Less common but more severe side effects include:

Because of the risk of side effects, it’s important to check in regularly with a healthcare professional. Additionally, it’s important to discuss any concerns you have about potential side effects with your doctor or other healthcare professional to make sure the medication is right for you.

When you lose a lot of weight quickly, your body loses fat, but it also loses lean mass, including muscle and bone density. This is problematic because muscle is the “engine” of your metabolism, helping you burn energy even when you are resting.

Research shows that people taking GLP-1 medications can lose a significant amount of muscle alongside fat. For example, in studies, about 15% to 40% of the total weight lost was lean mass. Exercise, such as strength training, can help preserve and build muscle while the medication helps you lose fat.

Exercise is also vital for bone health. Rapid weight loss is often linked to a reduction in bone mineral density, which can make bones weaker and more prone to fractures later in life.

A 2024 analysis of a randomized clinical trial found that people using the GLP-1 liraglutide without exercising lost weight but had decreased bone density in the hips and spine. People who combined liraglutide with regular exercise experienced the best weight loss and preserved their bone mineral density.

Exercise also has a lot of other benefits that GLP-1 medications can’t provide, like:

When used along with a balanced diet and exercise, Mounjaro can be an effective off-label treatment for weight loss and long-term weight management. How quickly the drug starts to work and the amount of weight loss can vary between people.

To learn more about what to expect when using Mounjaro for weight loss, talk with your doctor. They can tell you how soon you may see results and help determine what a safe weight-loss goal is for you based on your specific health factors.

#8990. Why I Lug My Own Props to Yoga Class

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

I had been practicing yoga for years before I discovered the magic of lugging my own mat to class.

Before that, I’d simply borrowed the cheap but convenient studio mats that were available for use. I considered myself too lazy to grapple with a heavy mat as I hauled it from the car to the studio and back again. But following some serious thought about functionality and germ exposure after I ended up with plantar warts (I mean, think about it), I decided it was worth the trouble to practice on my own sturdy mat.

And it was. I found more stability in standing poses from the mat’s refusal to slide or wrinkle on the floor, benefited from its extra grippiness in twists and backbends, and appreciated its additional cushioning in seated poses. It’s no exaggeration to say practicing on my own mat revolutionized my studio experience.

But I didn’t stop there. Following that experience, I began to look askance at other props in the studio—namely, blankets, bolsters, blocks, and straps—which appeared as broken in (or broken down?) as those loaner mats. And, I suspected, just as germy.

So I started bringing my own props—and my own germs—to class. Well, within reason. No sandbags or headstand bench, obviously. But I did load myself up before each class with the basics, including a blanket, strap, and block. If I was heading to a yin or restorative class, I brought my own bolster, too. I’d find my own comfort and marinate in my own sweat, thank you.

I’ve been doing this for 20 years. Beyond basic hygiene, the benefits of using my own props include functionality. Before you say blocks are blocks and blankets are blankets, they come in a dizzying array of shapes and materials, not to mention designs and colors. Do I want a foam block? Wood? Cork? Recycled materials? Purple? Pink? Black? Would my hands rather settle on a support that is rectangular, circular, oval, or square?

And as for a blanket, am I more of a pressed wool “yoga blanket” person or is a pretty “Mexican blanket” more my style? And don’t get me started on bolsters, with nearly infinite options for shapes and styles.

When I curate my DIY yoga props each class, I’m arming myself with props that I’ve worked with before and that strategically suit my body and take me even further into my practice. And because they are set to my preferences, I know them well enough to put them to effective use in a nanosecond.

My strap, for instance, is knotted in strategic locations, including one that makes it easy for me to reel in an errant back leg in my much-practiced Natarajasana (Dancer Pose). When that stays consistent from class to class, it makes it easier for me to find my version of the posture, which in turn means my focus can remain on the demands of the pose rather than fumbling with a strap or figuring out the height to adjust my block.

And although it’s about so much more than looks, it’s also about the looks. I just like having something pretty and functional and familiar surrounding me during my practice. My black mat, purple knotted strap, cork block, and wildly beautiful purple, orange, and teal bolster fit me to a T.

What matters is that by the time I’ve arranged the props around my mat, I’ve built what looks and feels like a cocoon of comfort. I’m no longer practicing in a gym-like room with a bunch of strangers. Rather, it’s as if I’m in my own private studio with my own private equipment among my own private germs. Yoga feels best when it also feels safe.

#8989. 13 Black Women Share How They Found the Strength to Survive—and Thrive—With Breast Cancer

When it comes to Black women’s breast health, the statistics rarely tell a hopeful story. Black women are diagnosed with breast cancer at a younger median age (60, compared with 62 for white women) and are 38% more likely to die from the disease. They have the lowest survival rate for every known stage of breast cancer. And about one in five Black women with breast cancer are diagnosed with hard-to-treat triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), more than any other racial or ethnic group.

But here’s what the numbers will never capture: the phone calls at 3 a.m., the head-shaving parties, the therapy sessions that cracked something open, the moment a woman looks at her daughter or granddaughter and decides they are reason enough to fight. Black women have always been more than a data point, and perhaps nowhere is that truer than in the way they face, survive, and remake their lives after a breast cancer diagnosis.

The stories below belong to 13 Black women who refused to be reduced to a statistic. They are individuals with careers, children, humor, faith, rage, and joy whose experiences with breast cancer changed them in ways both devastating and profound. In finding their own paths through treatment and beyond, they’ve built something the data can’t quantify: community, purpose, and a hard-won blueprint for survival they’re passing on to every woman who comes after them.

Monique Bass, 53, had always been proactive about her health. A single mother of twin sons and grandmother of four, she started getting annual mammograms at 40. But it was a self-exam at 47 while lying in bed one night that changed everything. She found a lump that didn’t feel right.

What followed were three tissue biopsies of the lump over three years, each coming back benign. Doctors wanted to keep monitoring. Bass pushed back. The lump was growing, and she knew her body well enough to realize something was wrong. She insisted they remove the lump (a procedure called a lumpectomy) and test it. The diagnosis: stage 1 invasive ductal carcinoma that was aggressive enough to require immediate chemotherapy.

Bass got the call while sitting in a car wash. “I felt like I was in The Twilight Zone,” she says. “Not in a million years did I think I would ever hear the words, ‘You have cancer.’” The timing made everything harder. It was 2020, the height of the pandemic, so she navigated much of her journey alone. Adding “another emotional layer,” she was also going through a divorce. Treatment included four rounds of doxorubicin, four rounds of paclitaxel, and 21 radiation treatments. Losing her hair hit the hardest. “But the silver lining is that it grew back even more beautifully after treatment,” Bass says.

Throughout it all her faith anchored her. “I’m not a deeply religious person, but I believe in God, and I knew he had me in the palm of his hand,” Bass says. On the other side of treatment, she founded What’s Behind the Bra?, a New Jersey nonprofit that distributes comfort care packages to breast cancer patients year-round and hosts a weekly podcast of the same name every Sunday at 7:30 p.m. ET.

Jaqueline Beale, 64, comes from a family with a long history of cancer, including her mother, who had breast cancer. That’s why it wasn’t a huge surprise when, at 40, she found a lump during a breast self-exam. Even though a sonogram and mammogram came back clear, it was obvious that something wasn’t right, so Beale got a biopsy.

When the radiologist called with her result—stage 1 breast cancer, which means the cancer hadn’t spread beyond where the abnormal cells had developed—she could hear a lot of noise in the background. He said, “I’m in New York trying to hail a cab, but you have breast cancer. You need to find a breast surgeon.” Despite the bluntness, Beale says she couldn’t help but find the humor in the situation, which is something she carried with her through treatment.

“I made sure that I surrounded myself with laughter and love,” she says, “and I told my family that I knew they loved me, but I also needed a lot of laughter to get through it.”

She recalls one incident in an elevator after her sister had taken her to a chemo treatment. “I had been sick as a dog after, and a woman got in and asked if I was okay. My sister said, ‘Oh, she’s fine. She’s just got a little bit of cancer.’ The woman looked horrified, but I laughed. My family knew that their sense of humor is what I needed.”

Annita White, 51, was five months late for her mammogram. As a single mother of two boys, a higher education administrator, and a first-year PhD student, she always had something more pressing. When she finally went, she expected the usual letter in the mail saying everything was fine. Instead, she got a call. There was a mass that hadn’t been there before.

By the time the biopsy came back, she already knew. A technician had commented on how hard the mass was, and White felt the diagnosis in her spirit before the words were ever spoken. The confirmation came the next day. “When I got the call, I fell to the floor and cried tears of desperation,” she says. “My first thought was, ‘Lord, I can’t do this.’”

What followed was hard in every way: chemotherapy, losing her breasts, losing her hair, which had always been full. “Being bald left me feeling vulnerable and insecure,” White says. “Physically, losing my breasts and going through chemotherapy made me feel like my body was no longer my own.” Through it all the fear that drove her was running out of time—time to see her sons become men and to meet her grandchildren someday.

Her faith, which she’d been privately wrestling with for years, met her exactly where she was. She’d been asking God to truly show up in her life. “He did,” she says. “In the middle of one of the hardest seasons of my life, he carried me through.”

Three years later White is cancer-free, her hair is back, and she recently finished her PhD. She now walks in her purpose as Dr. Nita, a member of the African American Breast Cancer Alliance survivor network, sharing her story and those of others facing the disease. “What once felt like the end became the beginning of something greater,” she says.

Marylande Regis, 38, had been in her new Georgia home for four months when everything changed. A registered nurse, realtor, wife, and mother of three, she had just stopped breastfeeding her nine-month-old when she found the lump. Her baby had never latched well on that side. When she messaged her provider, the on-call response was that it was probably a clogged milk duct and that she was too young to worry about it being something more serious. Regis didn’t accept that. She called back and left a message, insisting that something was wrong. “Another ob-gyn saw the message and encouraged me to make an office appointment immediately,” she says. Within two weeks she had a diagnosis: aggressive stage 2B, BRCA1-positive breast cancer. Within two more weeks what had been one tumor and one impacted lymph node had become three tumors and four impacted lymph nodes. Regis was 36.

“I was relieved that I advocated for myself,” she says. “I was proud that fear didn’t factor into my decision.”

What followed was relentless. Regis went through six months of chemotherapy, a bilateral mastectomy, six weeks of radiation, a total hysterectomy (to eliminate her body’s main source of estrogen), and breast reconstruction, all over a span of roughly 18 months. She lost friends to cancer along the way, as well as a cousin diagnosed around the same time. Her faith was, as Regis describes it, “shaken and stirred and flipped every way possible.” She wrote the important letters. She wrote her own obituary. She was practical about it. “I wanted to be positive, but I am also very realistic,” Regis says.

The hardest part wasn’t any single treatment—it was losing control. As her family’s go-to planner for everything from doctor’s appointments to vacations, she found it foreign to ask for help. But when she told her parents, her mother showed up and never left. “We joke, but my mom never went home,” Regis says. “This is her house now.” Her husband, Kory, came to every appointment and held steady even through both of them losing their jobs. “He deserves a trophy,” she says.

As the daughter of Haitian immigrants, raised to be everything her parents couldn’t be, Regis says the fight was never just medical. Today strength looks different than it did before cancer. It looks like making it to the bus stop with her son, who has autism. It looks like seeing her oldest finish nursing school and work toward becoming an ob-gyn. It looks like watching her youngest hit milestones like learning to talk. “I would have missed that if I didn’t fight,” she says. “The clouds are moving. The sun has decided to show itself. I can’t wait to soak it all in.”

Illness had always been an afterthought for 75-year-old Judy Fambrough-Billingsley. Why would it cross her mind? She walked three miles every day, swam laps all summer, took Zumba classes, and played soccer for 30 years. Judy Fambrough-Billingsley had never smoked or drank, and she didn’t even need to take medication. Being healthy wasn’t something she worked at; it was just who she was. A naturalized American citizen born in Germany, she traveled back to her home country regularly to visit family. Her life was full and active.

So when she felt a lump—and then another six months later—she ignored them. After all, she’d had a clean mammogram earlier that year. But when she noticed them growing and multiplying, she went back to her doctor. The results were not what she expected.

“I was shocked,” Fambrough-Billingsley says. She suddenly found herself navigating an entirely new set of experiences: prescription bottles, hospital procedures, lab processes—the whole medical system. “Being a part of a world where sickness exists had never been my world until now,” she says.

What carried her through was far older than her diagnosis. She grew up during the Civil Rights Era, the daughter of a successful Black entrepreneur who built his business during tumultuous years in US history. Both her parents were lifetime members of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). She was president of the NAACP Youth Council and an active member of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Fambrough-Billingsley knows something about fighting for your life in systems that weren’t built for you.

“Growing up during the Civil Rights Era contributed to this era of fighting,” she says. “Never giving up.” That same spirit—the one her parents modeled, the one she fell into during her work as a community organizer and across decades of a life fully lived—is the one she’s bringing to this too. She may still be on her breast cancer journey, but this is not her first fight.

Taylor Johnson was nearly 30 when she found the lump on her left breast. A mom and content creator who loves trying new things and staying active, she went to her primary care doctor, who referred her for an ultrasound and a mammogram. Johnson was denied a mammogram—she was told she was too young. She pushed anyway, got a biopsy (in lieu of the mammogram), and days later, had a diagnosis: stage 2 triple-negative breast cancer.

“My reaction was a very deep pause, trying to process what my doctor had told me,” Johnson says. “It then hit me, and all I could do was cry.”

She’s in the middle of her treatment plan, which includes six months of chemotherapy, followed by surgery and three weeks of radiation. After finishing chemo Johnson felt confident that would be the hardest part of her journey, both physically and emotionally. But her own health wasn’t her only concern: She knew her five-year-old was watching her every move, and she wanted to stay stable for her daughter. “I was so used to always being the strong one,” Johnson says. “This definitely tested that.” She held it together not because it came easily, but because she understood what her daughter was absorbing.

She is grateful for the community that rallied around her while she waited. Weekly prayer calls, rotating visits from family and friends, and a medical team at Mayo Clinic in Arizona that went above and beyond carried her through.

Though Johnson hasn’t finished treatment yet, completing chemo clarified something for her. “It has reassured me how strong I truly am,” she says. Strength, she’s learned, isn’t just physical. The emotional and mental muscle it takes to keep going counts just as much.

Jessica Ncube, 41, built her life around caring for others. A licensed clinical social worker, the co-owner of a mental health practice, and a mom, she was always in motion. Her life revolved around showing up for others and helping them navigate their hardest moments. “Looking back I do not know that I was always receiving,” she says.

Her diagnosis came quietly. A routine mammogram caught it; nothing in her body had felt amiss. That silence, Ncube says, is exactly why early detection matters. When she got the news she went into survival mode. “You hear the words, but it takes time for them to land,” she says.

Ncube’s journey started with a lumpectomy. When her margins came back unclear, meaning the pathologist could not determine whether all the cancerous cells were removed, she made the decision to move forward with a double mastectomy with reconstructive surgery. “Losing a part of your body, even when it is lifesaving, is still a loss,” she says. “The hardest part was learning how to sit in both gratitude and grief at the same time.”

As someone professionally wired to be strong for others, letting that tendency go was its own kind of work. “Strength became less about holding everything in and more about being honest about what I needed,” Ncube says. Her faith grounded her, and her community showed up, but she also had to unlearn something deeply familiar. “As a Black woman there is a resilience that is almost ingrained in us,” she says. “I had to learn how to balance that resilience with softness.”

After completing treatment Ncube has become more present and deliberate. Her definition of strength has changed entirely. “Strength today is softness. It is honesty. It is allowing myself to receive, to rest, and to not have all the answers,” she says.

Ameiko Newman, 40, didn’t learn of her diagnosis through a routine screening. She was rushed to the hospital for abdominal pain, and that’s when she learned she had breast cancer. Life before her diagnosis had been stressful, uncertain, a season of not quite knowing where she was headed. In a strange way, cancer gave her direction.

“For me, cancer saved me,” she says. “It made me a better person. It made me fight harder, push through the hard times and know what I want in life.”

Newman is still in treatment, receiving chemotherapy and immunotherapy every week, and she is honest about what that looks like: There are good days and bad days. She goes to church faithfully, prays every day, and tries to stay positive through it all.

What has surprised her most is that in the middle of fighting for her own life, she found her purpose: helping others fight for theirs. Newman rebranded her business entirely around that mission and started designing scarves with chemo patients in mind. “I started making them mainly for my Black women because you know we love having style,” she says. But a wide variety of women from all over have since bought them.

She wakes up every day, gets her kids ready, works out, and moves through life. Faith, she says, is what makes that possible. Her message to any Black woman who’s just gotten diagnosed is both simple and hard-won: “Cancer doesn’t define you. You define you. Even though you’re fighting for your life, help someone else fight for theirs.”

Charlotte Connor, 38, had just undergone a breast augmentation when she felt a lump in her breast. “When I saw my doctor, they weren’t concerned, in part because of my young age,” says Connor, who was 30 years old at the time. She had a mammogram and ultrasound to check for signs of cancer, but no MRI. “Looking back now I wish I would have asked for that MRI,” she says.

At the first checkup six months later, they told her she was fine. At the second—one year after the original lump was found—the lump had tripled in size. Her doctor ordered a biopsy, and her diagnosis was confirmed: stage 2A ductal carcinoma, which means the cancer was growing but contained to the breast and surrounding lymph nodes.

“When they told me I had cancer, I was calm,” she says. Her mindset immediately shifted from a sinking feeling to being optimistic about the future. “I focused on getting healthy again,” says Connor, who started fantasizing about what she would do after treatment.

She remembers thinking, I may be feeling sick and throwing up from chemotherapy, but what restaurants am I going to go to after all this is over? It’s an outlook that didn’t necessarily come naturally to her, either. “I’m not even overly optimistic in life—I think I’m a realist—but in this situation, I shifted to being overly optimistic.”

Part of that mindset shift was for her young daughter. “I couldn’t be pessimistic; I had to be strong for her,” she says. “And I knew that how I acted in this situation was how she was going to mirror things and react to stressful situations when she got older.”

Connor’s other pillar of support came from a tight-knit circle of friends and family, who threw her a head-shaving party before she lost her hair due to chemo. “Making things fun and lighthearted like that got me through my darkest, saddest moments,” she says.

It was 1999, and Donna Culmer had just received a clean mammogram. A few months later she felt a stone-size bump on her right side, so she went back to her ob-gyn to get it checked out. They redid the mammogram on both breasts, and while what she’d felt was actually a fibrocystic lump, the imaging found a small, not palpable spot on her left side that turned out to be a stage 1 cancer. “I was stunned,” Culmer says. “I didn’t even know what questions to ask.” She drove back to work in a daze and told her boss what had happened.

At 46 she was serving in the Navy as an instructor and trainer to personnel who were working alongside the Marines. She was married to a Marine and raising three children. There was no good moment for this. There never is.

Four months of chemotherapy followed, with nausea and exhaustion that never quite let up. Her doctors were concerned that the chemo might not work, so she had a mastectomy. Through it all her community refused to let her go through it alone. Her father drove her to every session and sat with her. Her church came to her, literally; services were held at her house.

Twenty-seven years later, Culmer, now 73, has had time to reflect. “As Black women, we have been through challenges our whole lives,” she says. “This is just one more.” Her advice is practical and clear. “Don’t panic and ask questions, even if you have to write them down,” Culmer says. “The treatments available now are so much better than what I had.”

One morning, Patricia Fox, 38, woke up with a lump in her right breast that wasn’t there the night before—she was just 26 years old at the time. Fox scheduled an appointment with her ob-gyn that day. “They told me that I was a young Black woman and had dense breasts, and it was likely a cyst,” she says. “They were ready to turn me away.”

The lump, which was a little smaller than a golf ball, seemed strange to Fox. Thankfully, she listened to her intuition. “There was something telling me to get it checked out,” she says, so her doctor did a biopsy just to be sure.

Her results came back as estrogen receptor-positive stage 2A breast cancer, meaning her cancer had estrogen receptors that would respond to hormone therapy drugs. Fox says she’ll never forget her doctor’s words: “Patricia, you’ll be a breast cancer survivor.” That sentiment set the tone for her mindset as a fighter. “It made me think that I could face this and survive this,” she says.

Still, cancer treatments quickly overwhelmed Fox, and soon she faced her lowest point: crying on the floor for hours, feeling like having cancer at such a young age was a punishment for being a “bad person.” But she pulled herself out of it with hard work in therapy.

“I found that talking to a therapist helped me process my diagnosis and examine the areas of my life—certain people and my own behavior patterns—that were cancerous for me that I needed to do something about,” she says. “While therapy didn’t make the pain go away, it did make how I coped with it much better.”

In the Black community, therapy is often taboo, says Fox, but it’s become her mission to dispel that belief. “Therapy fortified me to get through cancer,” she says, “and I tell everyone that they don’t have to suffer in silence.”

Annette Colden, 63, was sitting at her sister’s bedside during the last days of her final battle with breast cancer when the conversation turned to screenings. Her sister had been through cervical cancer and two bouts of breast cancer before passing away from the disease. “She made me promise I’d get my mammograms,” Colden says.

Colden’s first two yearly mammograms were clear. On the third there was a spot, but she was told by her doctor that things looked okay and it wasn’t cancer—she just had lumpy breasts.

“There’s this inner feeling you have,” she says. “Something was inside me saying, That’s not right.” Her sister’s doctor had told her the exact same thing, but Colden was so happy to hear she didn’t have cancer that she didn’t follow up.

A year later she went back for a mammogram, and that’s when her doctors found it: stage 0 breast cancer, meaning only abnormal cells had been found. She was 42. “Now, looking back, I always tell women that if something doesn’t feel right, get a second opinion.”

Despite the diagnosis Colden remained calm. “I’m a religious person,” she says. “In my prayer I said, ‘Lord, if you will be my pilot on this journey, I’ll be your copilot.’” She immediately felt a sense of peace.

After her recovery she decided to share that calming presence with other women going through breast cancer at a support group through Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, where she had treatment. “I say, ‘It’s going to be a long road. If you don’t want to travel it alone, I’m right there with you.’”

And she means it. Sometimes that involves talking with someone at 3 a.m. when the pain from chemotherapy hits. Other times it means sending food delivery boxes to the homes of people with breast cancer who can’t muster the strength to leave. “My sister did a lot of support work before she got really sick,” she says. “This is her vision.”

Ricki Fairley, 69, was in the security line at the airport for a work trip when she got a call from her doctor. They’d found a peanut-like lump under her nipple that turned out to be cancer.

Fairley, who was 55 at the time, said, “I don’t have time for this right now. I’ll call you when I get to my destination.” A couple days later she found out she had stage 3A TNBC, and it was really aggressive. Compared with other breast cancers, TNBC has fewer targeted-therapy treatment options, often spreads beyond the breasts, and is more likely to recur. Black women have nearly three times the risk of developing triple-negative breast cancer.

Her diagnosis woke her up. “It made me realize that I needed to get all of the ‘cancers’ out of my life,” Fairley says. During treatment that first year which involved a double mastectomy, aggressive chemotherapy, and radiation, she quit her job and started her own company. Then she filed for divorce and later sold her house. “I quit my life and started a new one, and changed everything,” she says. “I had to learn that my peace is nonnegotiable. I really think that stress caused my breast cancer.”

A year later her life changed again. Fairley was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer and told she had two years to live. After finding out her current doctor had only treated two previous cases of TNBC and both women had died in eight months, she found a new doctor, who was well-versed in current research and treatments for the disease. She beat cancer a second time. “I remember sitting at my daughter’s graduation thinking, Okay, I made it. What’s next for me?” Fairley says. The answer: helping others. In the years that followed, Fairley cofounded The Black Breast Cancer Alliance, which works to reduce the mortality rate for Black women.

Whenever you’re taking CBD or THC, keep these factors in mind.

There are three different types of CBD: isolates, broad-spectrum, and full-spectrum. Full spectrum CBD products contain THC which can trigger an entourage effect in some people.

However, it’s important to note that CBD and THC can work one way in one person, but works a different way in the next person.

The effects THC has can vary greatly from one person to another, even if it’s a smaller dose. Lower doses generally may help you relax while higher doses may make you feel anxious or paranoid.

CBD will not get you “high”, unlike it’s cousin THC. Experts generally recognize CBD as safe, though there are some side effects that may occur, like fatigue, diarrhea, appetite changes, and weight changes.

There is some research that suggests CBD may interact with the liver, potentially interfering with the metabolism of other medications. If you take any medications or supplements, talk with a healthcare professional before taking any CBD or THC products.

Research notes that THC can induce symptoms of psychosis in people who do not already have the condition, and THC at high doses can increase anxiety. Other research also cautions against THC use if you have cardiovascular or respiratory conditions.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA)Trusted Source warns that THC can pose health risks and causes adverse effects like hallucinations, tremors, anxiety, and more.

Stricter legislation is coming in, and it may affect access to CBD and THC products. The federal government is changing how they define “hemp” at the federal level. The new definition seeks to ban hemp-derived THC, the cannabis compound that causes a “high.”

The current law states that hemp is any part of the cannabis sativa plant that contains up to 0.3% of THC by dry weight. The change will restrict any hemp-derived products to a total of 0.4 milligrams (mg) of THC per container. This is much stricter than the current law and will impact access to products with a higher THC content.

The new law also bans synthetic cannabinoids, affecting CBD manufacturing. Cannabinoids, like CBD or THC, occur naturally in the hemp plant. However, chemical synthesis is often necessary to make CBD available on a commercial level, and this is where we may see further restrictions.

States with established recreational and medical cannabis regulations may be less affected by the ban. Meanwhile, those without existing regulations, such as Texas and Kentucky, may see a bigger impact.

Full-spectrum and broad-spectrum CBD products are most likely to be affected as they contain trace amounts of THC.

The ban is currently due to take effect by mid-December. It’s unclear exactly how these changes will affect the industry, but until then, people can still purchase CBD THC gummies and other CBD products, like oils and topicals.

CBD gummies are not legal in all 50 states. A person should always check local laws before buying CBD gummies of any kind.

#8987. 8 Simple Yin Yoga Poses to Release Tension From Your Entire Body

This yin yoga for a full-body stretch routine includes relatively simple shapes with options that help you find your comfort level, even if you’re new to yin yoga. In this style of stretching, we hold shapes for an extended period of time, but we don’t use any kind of muscular effort. Yin yoga is not about getting stronger and it’s not about endurance. It’s about relaxing in all of the poses and letting gravity do the work for you to send the stretch into the joints as well as the connective tissues.

You’re always trying to find your edge in these poses, which means you’re not trying to be so intense that you need to tense your body or hold your breath. You should experience some sensation, but it should never ever feel painful. Especially because you want to be able to stay in each stretch for several minutes. Usually a yin yoga pose is held for three to five minutes, although if you’re a beginner, then start by staying for a little less time, because even two minutes can feel like an eternity!

Basically, yin yoga is meant to consist of simple shapes held for a little longer than usual, and you’ll definitely feel the difference by the end of it. Think of this as an introduction to yin yoga and know that there are so many more poses to explore.

You definitely don’t need props to practice yin yoga. But it can be helpful to know how to use them to experience more support in the poses, so for the following poses, I suggest you consider using props, whether two blocks and a strap or, if you don’t have those at home, you can use some pillows or couch cushions and a belt or even a sweatshirt. There are all sorts of everyday household items you can use in place of props.

Kneel on the mat, bring your big toes together, and then let your knees go apart. The wider your knees, the more intense the stretch through the inner thighs. You don’t want to cause any kind of pinching or compression in your lower back. If you feel tightness or tension there, it usually means your knees are too far apart and you simply need to bring them slightly closer together.

Walk your hands away from you and lean your chest toward the mat. You can either rest your forehead on the mat or stack your hands and use them or a pillow as support for your forehead in Child’s Pose. You can also bring a block or firm pillow lengthwise under your chest and forehead to close any gap between your body and the mat and then rest your body on that while turning your head to one side.

Try to let your hips be heavy as they sink toward your heels. Let your chest melt toward the mat or the support beneath you. Relax your arms and shoulders and upper back, and simply breathe slow and steady, in and out through your nose. Stay here for about 2 minutes.

When you’re ready to come out of the pose, bring your palms to the mat and press into them so you can start to lift your head and chest back up.

Slide forward onto your belly with your legs straight behind you. Try to keep your feet about hip-distance apart. Then bring your forearms in front of you with your elbows a little in front of your shoulders and your palms about shoulder-distance apart in Sphinx Pose.

You get to control how intense you make this backbend. The farther forward you bring your forearms, the easier the stretch across the front of your back and the less compression in your lower back. Alternatively, you can make the stretch a little more intense by bringing your elbows directly underneath your shoulders.

Now press your shoulders back a little, so you’re lightly squeezing your shoulder blades behind you. Keep your chin parallel to the floor and think about gently reaching your chest forward. If there’s pinching or compression or any kind of pain in your lower back, you know you’ve gone a little too far in the pose and you want to bring your arms a little more forward to lessen the backbend.

Feel your rib cage expand front to back and side to side with the rhythm of your breath. Stay here for about 2 minutes.

Very slowly release out of the pose and lower your chest back down to the mat.

Come to your hands and knees and you might want to keep your blocks within reach for this one. Step your right foot forward in between your palms in Low Lunge. I like to fold the left edge of the mat onto itself underneath my left knee to pad it since we’ll be here for a little while. You can also slide a folded blanket or pillow underneath your back knee.

Try to keep your right ankle underneath your right knee as you keep your hands on the mat or bring blocks underneath your palms. Then let your hips sink forward and down. Release the shoulders away from your ears and let gravity do the work for you here in this hip-opening stretch.

If you need to take any breaks, you’re welcome to straighten your front leg and release it. Otherwise, try to let yourself ease into the pose.

When you’re ready to come out of the pose, start to push down into your right heel to slowly lift yourself and bring yourself back to hands and knees. Before we repeat the same pose on the other side, it might feel good to do a few hip circles or take another brief Child’s Pose. Just notice the difference in how you feel from one side to the other.

This time, step your left foot forward in between your hands at the top of the mat and keep your hands to either side of that front foot while keeping your chest lifted. Try not to collapse your weight into your wrists. Keep pressing into the fingertips and knuckles.

When you’re ready to come out, come to a seat on the mat.

This is basically a seated forward fold. You’ll probably want to have your blocks handy for this one. Just extend your legs straight in front of you. You want your feet to be about hip-distance apart. Then lean forward in a Seated Forward Bend known as Caterpillar. In yin yoga, when you bend forward, you’re not pushing or pulling or forcing your way into a more intense stretch. In fact, you want to just let you back round and the rest of your body relax into the pose with very little effort. I like to turn my palms to face upward so I’m not tempted to push or pull my way deeper into the pose.

Your legs do not need to be perfectly straight. You can absolutely bend your knees if that’s more comfortable for you. Let yourself relax into the pose, including your neck. If your chest is somewhere close to the mat, you might want to prop yourself up with a block either under your chest or forehead. If your chest is a little more upright, you can use both blocks stacked beneath you so you have some support.

You might feel the stretch along the entire back of the body, from the head down the spine and all the way into the back of the legs to the heels. The longer you stay in this pose, the more you might notice that your body might slip a little deeper into the stretch. The pose tends to change quite a little the longer we hold it. Simply stay here and see what happens.

When you’re ready to lift yourself out of the pose, go extra slowly since forward folds can be quite intense for the low back. Start by flipping your palms, pushing your hands into the mat, and using arm strength to lift yourself, inch by inch. You’re really not rushing this. Keep breathing evenly as you transition out of the poses.

Keep your left leg straight in front of you and bend your right knee. Bring your right foot across your body and rest it on the mat to the outside of your left thigh. Grab your right knee with your left hand and start to turn your chest toward the right, bringing your right fingertips behind your right hip, and continue to twist toward the right as you squeeze your right thigh toward your belly.

Try to eliminate any rounding in your spine. Think instead of grounding into the mat and, at the same time, reaching the crown of the head toward the ceiling while releasing your shoulders down and away from your ears. So you want to be lengthening through the spine a little more each time you inhale. Maybe you close your eyes, paying attention to your breath in and out through your nose.

When you’re ready to release, slowly unwind and face forward. Then switch sides, extending your right leg straight in front of you, bending your left knee and crossing your left foot over your right thigh. And then twist and rotate the spine from there, hugging the belly toward the spine.

When you’re ready, unwrap and face forward again.

Grab your strap and lower all the way down onto your back. Bend your knees and bring your feet flat on the mat about hip-distance apart. Bring your right knee toward your chest and drape the strap around the ball of your right foot. Then extend your right leg straight toward the ceiling.

My favorite way to do this reclined hamstring stretch is instead of actively reaching my arms to hold the strap, I let my upper arms relax against the mat. Then I don’t need to use quite as much arm strength.

Let your right leg be soft and relaxed, using just a little arm strength to guide the leg toward your chest. Just like in your seated forward fold, you can absolutely bend your right knee. If you’d like to make this stretch a little more sensational, slide your left leg straight on the mat. Sometimes the lifted leg will shake a little, and that’s usually just a sign that you’re taking the pose a little too far.

To come out of the pose, bend your right knee and remove the strap. Then switch sides. Wrap the strap around your left foot, extend your left leg straight up, and find your stretch.

When you’re ready, slowly release the strap and remain lying on your back.

So our next pose is one of my all-time favorite yin yoga poses. It’s called Banana Pose for reasons you’ll understand shortly. It’s a great way to open the sides of your body.

Stay on your back and shimmy your hips as far over toward the right of the mat as you can. Then bring your shoulders and your chest a little more toward the left. Extend your legs straight, and then inch your ankles toward the left in a banana shape.

You can reach your arms overhead and rest them wherever is comfortable or bend your elbows and hold onto opposite forearms. Try to keep your right hip grounded to the floor as much as possible.

If you want a slightly more intense stretch, cross your right ankle over your left ankle. You will probably feel a nice opening along the waist, hip, and along the IT band along your outer thigh. Sometimes it takes a little readjusting until you can find the sweet spot where it’s not too intense and not too hard to hold. You want it to be comfortable enough that you could stay here for a few minutes without having to readjust.

Try to send your breath to the right side of your body, filling up the space you’re creating, and relaxing into the pose a little more with every exhalation.

If you had your ankles crossed, you can let that go. Then we’re going to ease into the stretch on the other side, shifting your hips over to the left side of the mat  while the upper body moves to the right, and then reaching with your upper body as well.

You might want your blocks for this one. Still lying on your back, bring the soles of your feet together to touch. Make sure your shoulders and your hips are in line, and let your knees open wide. If the lower back or the hips feel really tight, you can use your blocks beneath your knees or thighs so there’s a little support here, which will make the pose easier. Otherwise, you can just let your legs fall open and let your arms rest wherever is comfortable. You can even reach your arms alongside your head if you want to stretch the shoulders and upper back. Send your breath all the way down to your low belly and low back.

When you’re ready to come out of the pose, you can use your hands to help your knees come back together or you can settle straight into the next pose.

In this last pose, straighten your legs in front of you and slightly out to the sides, and let your body take up space. Rest your arms somewhere comfortable, palms facing upward, and just let yourself release into the shape. Maybe you quietly notice the effects of your practice on your body, your mind, and your breath. Release any tension in your facial muscles and your jaw and simply let yourself be.

When you’re ready, begin to lengthen your breath as you slowly wake back up. Maybe you wiggle your fingers and toes or circle your wrists and ankles. Let your head slowly turn from side to side. Then take a stretch by extending your arms overhead. Eventually, you can slowly sit up nice and tall, closing your eyes. Bring your hands together at the front of the chest and simply notice what feels differently. Thank you for doing this beginner yin yoga for a full-body stretch with me. I hope you enjoyed it. Let me know what you think in a comment below.

#8986. Is it too late to start strength training at 70? (No. Here’s what happens when you do.)

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s get meaningfully stronger when they start strength training, and beginners tend to see the biggest response to training.

You also need far less than you’d guess: 30 to 60 minutes of lifting spread across a week is a great starting point.

Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.

A reader wrote me this week. Her whole email was one sentence:

That hits deep. That fear of: have I missed my window?

I want to share with you what I shared with her, because the science behind this is actually super cool and empowering.

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s still get stronger when they start lifting. And it meaningfully improves how they move through their lives.

And if you’re someone who hasn’t trained before, or hasn’t trained in a while, I have even better news.

As a beginner, your body is even more sensitive to training. Translation: you get even more reward for your effort!

In the first few weeks, most people feel stronger before they look any different.

That’s because a lot of early strength is actually your muscles and brain learning to coordinate. The movement gets smoother. Standing up from a chair feels a little easier. Etc.

Over a few months, muscle starts to build.

Your bones respond to the load too (strength training is one of the best-supported ways to support bone health as we age.)

You’ll start to feel some muscle in your arms that you didn’t notice there before, like this reader who’s been doing workouts 3x/week and kicking butt with it:

Is every body different? Yes. Does it also depend on sleep, nutrition, and what else life is throwing at you? Also yes.

But the direction is the same for everyone. No matter your age, you can make a meaningful impact in your overall health, fitness, and quality of life!

1) Don’t start with workouts. Start with practice.

Take a few minutes each day to learn and practice a couple of strength moves.

You’re not training yet. You’re getting acquainted.

Try some push-ups off of the wall or the countertop. ​ Sit down in a chair, slow and controlled, and practice keeping your weight evenly spread across your feet (that’s a squat right there!)

Grab a gallon jug, some light dumbbells or canned goods or whatever you have on hand, and practice a one-arm row. See if you can feel it in your upper back as you pull the weight up.

Work within whatever your ability level is, what feels safe and approachable to start.

You’re collecting information about what your body is ready for, and learning exercises like you’re learning a new skill.

30-60 minutes of strength training in TOTAL across the week goes a surprisingly long way.

You can break that up however works best for you. A short 5-10min session most days of the week, inserting some “movement snacks” throughout the day, or a couple of longer sessions 2x/week, etc.

It doesn’t require hours of your day to make serious progress.

3) It’s easier to level up than to cut down

Because your body is more sensitive to strength training, you’ll likely feel more sore in the beginning.

So in general, I recommend you err on the side of less is more.

If you do a few short sessions during the week, and wake up the next day feeling great with little to no soreness, great! You can add a bit more the next week.

Mentally, I’ve also just found it’s way easier to be “leveling up” than having to cut back, which really helps with building that early momentum.

Becky, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, is someone I immediately thought of when I read that initial email. She’s 77, and didn’t start going to the gym until she was 57. Here’s what she had to say:

I couldn’t have said it any better myself, Becky. 😊

No matter your age or where you’re starting from…YOU GOT THIS! 💪

Whenever you’re ready, here are more ways we can help

1) Here’s an article with a bunch of different bodyweight exercises and progressions you can do at home.

2) Our coaches build programs specific to you and your needs. Here’s the exact system we use.

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

Humans featured are exceptional examples and do not guarantee individual success. Your experience and results may vary.

#8985. If You Don’t Practice Yoga in the Morning, You Might Be Missing Out. Here’s What Science Says.

When I first started practicing online yoga to address the tightness and discomfort I was experiencing from sitting all day, I snuck yoga into my schedule literally whenever I could. Noon. After work. Before bed.

But the more I scrolled for practices, the more I noticed one theme showing up again and again. Namely, morning yoga. Curious, I searched YouTube for “morning yoga” and found literally thousands of videos. Yoga with Kassandra has an entire Morning Yoga playlist featuring more than 238 videos, some of which have drawn more than two million views each. Yoga With Adriene has a “Morning Mobility Yoga” video from a couple years ago that was just shy of 10 million views. That got me wondering whether there are more benefits of morning yoga as opposed to practicing it at other times of day. Being a night owl, I found that I was most likely to unroll my mat in the evenings. Should I change my habits?!

Turns out, the answer is complicated. There are definite benefits of morning yoga, yet a lot depends on why you’re practicing yoga as well as your personal quirks.

There’s been a surprising amount of scientific research on the benefits of morning yoga. And let’s not overlook the fact that, historically, many yoga traditions favored practicing yoga in the early morning. I mean, take Sun Salutations, which is a sequence of poses, or asana, performed facing east as the sun peeps over the horizon. And depending on your schedule and your personality, there can also be practical reasons.

There’s a very real possibility of becoming so distracted or delayed by work or life that practicing yoga doesn’t happen at all if it doesn’t happen in the morning. Just ask anyone who’s ever intended to make a late-afternoon studio class but ended up stuck at work or feeling too defeated by the day to crawl onto their mat.

Yet the evidence for this anecdotal experience is limited. Research on exercise adherence is inconclusive in terms of whether morning or evening is better, with some research suggesting that practicing at a consistent time of day is more relevant than the exact time of day. But if you do unroll your mat in the morning, even if your day falls off the rails, at least you gave yourself yoga beforehand.

If you can find time to make it onto your mat later in the day, one study suggests mental distraction is more of an issue during evening practices. Whether the distractions take the shape of ruminating over the day or contemplating the things that still need to be accomplished before night’s end, it’s possible you will encounter fewer distractions in the mornings.

And although bringing yourself back to a quiet mind is the purpose of yoga, perhaps you don’t need any additional challenges in that realm.

One study suggests that daily morning yoga supported “emotional well-being” more than less frequent evening yoga participation. This was tested across two groups: one that attended Ashtanga yoga classes at 7 am for two work weeks; the second practiced Ashtanga yoga at night once or twice from Monday to Friday for two weeks. Though both groups had practiced in the evening previously, the morning group experienced greater change after the two-week study.

Of course, the increased frequency of practicing five times a week might have also affected the participants. More yoga is usually better than less.

A recent 2026 study on morning versus evening online yoga found that practicing early in the day (6 to 7 am) was better than evening yoga (6 to 7 pm) in terms of effects on sleep and lifestyle in a group of young adults. Specifically, they found that morning yoga improved energy and restfulness. It also enhanced participants’ self-reported psychological health over the course of the four-week study.

An earlier study also found that practicing morning yoga can help minimize morning sleepiness.

If you’re someone who likes your yoga vigorous, stick with morning sessions. A 2024 review of multiple studies found that, overall, more intense activity, including yoga, at night could easily disrupt sleep. Morning sessions didn’t have the same effect.

Research is somewhat limited on the topic of morning yoga reducing stress. Yet a 2023 study compared morning yoga and gym practices (6 to 9 am) against evening yoga and gym practices (6 to 10 pm). The morning yoga group experienced lower cortisol than the morning gym workout group. The researchers theorized this supports feeling happier, more optimistic, and being able to pay attention and work with more efficiency throughout the day.”

As with much in life, there is no one-size-fits-all answer regarding when to practice yoga. The best yoga for you is the yoga that you’re actually going to do, whatever the time of day, style, intensity, and length. Although if you’re looking for a reason to make time to unroll your mat in the a.m., there are more than enough reasons to try it. Chances are, it won’t take long to experience the benefits yourself.

Economy isn't business class, but United's Pacific routes are comfortable — you'll find decent legroom in Economy Plus if you want to upgrade your seat selection for a modest fee, complimentary entertainment, and meal service on this longer domestic segment. The flight across the Pacific, even in economy, has a different feel than a 2-hour domestic hop. The water below you turns that impossible shade of blue. You land in Honolulu at mid-morning, cleared customs quickly (domestic flight — no customs required), and you're at your hotel before lunch.

Total cost for two one-way tickets: 15,000 miles + $22. Cash equivalent: $778. Money saved: $756. That's a car payment, a month of groceries, or a head start on your next investment contribution — redirected from airline revenue to your FI journey.

The 7,500-mile rate is available year-round — Turkish doesn't have a separate peak pricing tier for this redemption. But United's saver inventory dries up fast during summer, spring break, and the December holidays. Target September through November and January through mid-February for the best combination of availability and lower cash prices (which tells you demand is lower). Mid-week departures (Tuesday, Wednesday) consistently show better saver seat availability than weekend flights.

Turkish's booking window opens 355 days in advance. United releases the bulk of its saver award inventory when the schedule first opens — roughly 11 months before departure. If you have a specific date in mind (say, a milestone anniversary trip), start checking 355 days out and move fast when you see availability.

Book the outbound through Turkish (LAX→HNL, 7,500 miles) and then search for a separate return award. Turkish allows open-jaw itineraries, so you could theoretically fly into Honolulu and return from Maui if routing works. Piece together two one-way awards for maximum flexibility.

This is the single most common mistake. Points transfers to Turkish are irreversible. If you transfer 7,500 points and then discover saver availability has disappeared, those points are in Turkish's system with no easy path back. Always confirm availability on the Turkish booking portal before initiating any transfer.

Marriott Bonvoy transfers to Turkish at a 3:1 ratio and takes 1–5 days. You'd need 22,500 Marriott points to get 7,500 Turkish miles — a terrible rate. Stick with Citi ThankYou or Bilt at 1:1, both instant.

If you're combining this Hawaii redemption with an international Turkish itinerary, Turkish allows free stopovers in Istanbul on connecting itineraries. That's a separate strategy, but worth knowing as your travel portfolio grows.

Turkish miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Even one small miles transaction — earning or redeeming — resets the clock. Transfer a small batch of points or book a cheap award every few years to keep your account alive.
